It has been revealed that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

Industry observers note that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

In a recent development, there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Sources indicate that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint claims so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

In a recent development, the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

It has been revealed that here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

According to recent reports, also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

Sources indicate that setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

According to recent reports, now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Recent findings suggest that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to people later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

It has been revealed that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF indicates what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

Sources indicate that A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Recent findings suggest that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

Sources indicate that in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

It has been revealed that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

In a recent development, across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Recent findings suggest that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small upgrade to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

Like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

In a recent development, these AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

Sources indicate that to launch, tap the fresh pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”.

According to recent reports, this is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now quickly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • South Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices.
  • Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most important yearly events.
  • The brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

South Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices. The anti-cheating measure was declared after a cheater in South Korea’s tax accountant exam confessed to using AI and a micro-camera to cheat. The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most important yearly events. The exam is so significant that the whole country pauses and makes way for the test-takers; police clear the roads and escort late students, noisy construction and maintenance are suspended, aircraft are grounded, military exercises are paused, and the stock market opens an hour later. The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

The brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives. With such high stakes, cheating is not unusual.

It has been revealed that the month before the CSAT, South Korea’s Certified Tax Accountant exam received an unusually large number of high scorers — with 66 candidates scoring over 90+ in introductory accounting over only two in 2025 and one in 2024, as reported by The Korean Herald. The top scorer, Han Won-seok, confessed to cheating on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, admitting to cheating using a micro-camera that feeds images of the test to an AI on his smartphone.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

In a recent development, the first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

According to recent reports, alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. In July, Lee Jin-woo, a Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) candidate, achieved an impressive perfect score and is reportedly the first to do so. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

When the tax accountant cheater confessed on Sunday, it led to online suspicion about Lee’s perfect LEET score, with two lawyers even filing legal complaints accusing him of obstruction of official duties. Lee was supposed to be interviewed on YouTube early on Thursday to prove his academic abilities, but he did not show up. Later that day, when Police investigated the legal complaints and after he was reported missing, he was found dead of cardiac arrest at 1:12 PM in a motel, with a note at the scene stating he was mentally and physically exhausted, with no mention of the cheating allegations, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

このデータセットには、個人を特定できる情報（PII）は一切含まれていません。年齢、名前、職業などは公的な統計データの分布に基づいていますが、存命・故人問わず、実在の人物と結びつくことはありません。全てのペルソナは完全に人工的に生成されているため、実際の文化的パターンを保ちながらも、個人のプライバシーを損なうことなくトレーニングに利用できます。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japanは、日本のソブリン AI システムを開発する日本のモデル開発者向けに設計されています。現在、LLM開発者が使用する訓練データのほとんどは英語であり、日本やインドなど各地域の開発者は、母国語で高品質なデータを入手するのに苦労しています。.

本データセットを含め、NVIDIA の Nemotron-Personas の一連の取り組みは、こうした課題を直接解決するものです。地域固有のニュアンスを捉えつつ、開発者が地域固有の言語で多様かつ複雑なデータを生成できるようサポートします。データセットは国勢調査データ、日本人の命名規則、文化的特徴など地域のコンテキストに基づき、すべて母語で生成しています。.

VibeGame: Exploring Vibe Coding Games

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People are trying to vibe code games.
  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
  • According to recent reports, first, what is vibe coding?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

According to recent reports, first, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

Industry observers note that however, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

Sources indicate that earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very swiftly.

To address this concern, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

Recent findings suggest that I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Recent findings suggest that anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Recent findings suggest that beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

Recent findings suggest that I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

Sources indicate that the official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

Roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

In a recent development, the unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

This approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

It has been revealed that this will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

Recent findings suggest that here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

According to recent reports, so, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires owners to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

In a recent development, then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

Industry observers note that the engine is at the moment very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

It has been revealed that it's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what's going on in the space!

Thanks for the post ! If you have feedback or feature requests the Roblox MCP server, feel free to submit issues on the project page:.

Industry observers note that this is very cool! A mini-engine with API designed for LLMs may be able to supercharge game development.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone interested in exploring what's already being built, we've been collecting the best AI-Assisted and vibe-coded games on VibeTopList. Feel free to check for yourself https://vibetoplist.com/.

I've been working on something along similar lines, called Rosh.

It has been revealed that it covers some of the things you list as missing. Rooms are multiplayer and live: people and AI agents can be in the same room changing it together. The same room works in real time in your browser (three.js), a terminal, Unity and Unreal Engine. It also reads the room back to the AI as text, with notes on what looks wrong, so agents can fix their own object placement etc.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Sources indicate that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

Sources indicate that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly vital when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/owners.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Recent findings suggest that runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a newly introduced optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

Sources indicate that however, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Sources indicate that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a tech giant might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Recent findings suggest that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

According to recent reports, you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document key endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

Breaking: Accelerating Qwen3-8B Agent on Intel® Core™ Ultra with Depth-Pruned Draft Models

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

Recent findings suggest that qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

In a recent development, speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

Before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

The speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Our recent work reveals that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

Industry observers note that the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

According to recent reports, to showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

In a recent development, here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. This simple workflow highlights just a fraction of the possibilities unlocked when accelerated Qwen3 models meet frameworks like 🤗smolagents, bringing practical, efficient AI agents to life on AI PC. Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a newly introduced built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

It has been revealed that spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

Sources indicate that “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta patch, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp customers.

Tech Report: Introducing RTEB: A New Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a new benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • The performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • Sources indicate that this is where things get tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a new benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

The performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

Sources indicate that this is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on new, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following issues:.

Recent findings suggest that the Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

It has been revealed that because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to latest problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

In a recent development, misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these challenges are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a new, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

It has been revealed that this hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

Sources indicate that RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

In a recent development, A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We proposal to continually revision both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an matter on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

Sources indicate that RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we plan to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest new datasets, find challenges in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an issue in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our plans for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

The RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the latest Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

Recent findings suggest that [1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (currently denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

The discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets indicates why a single retrieval average can hide important differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

RTEB leaderboard have bm25 and some other baseline models https://leaderboard.mteb.org/benchmark/RTEB(beta)?pin=mteb%252Fbaseline-bm25s.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Industry observers note that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Recent findings suggest that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

According to recent reports, lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Recent findings suggest that base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every blueprint, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

It has been revealed that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

According to recent reports, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Industry observers note that replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

According to recent reports, core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

It has been revealed that bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web looks run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

According to recent reports, retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

It has been revealed that figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Sources indicate that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real organization data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

It has been revealed that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human owners.

It has been revealed that building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to customers.

The first was confirmed last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone.

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:.

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. The first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat users in the US and Canada that indicates “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out new Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

  • According to recent reports, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

According to recent reports, enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

According to recent reports, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In a recent development, in this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

Industry observers note that to follow along, clone the repo. You'll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:.

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:.

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

Dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

Recent findings suggest that when kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

Once we've done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:.

The model doesn't require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

Industry observers note that using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

In a recent development, you can check out the initial harness here. If we run the following on the original code implementation:.

It has been revealed that it is rare that a model will convert first time. Often, you will need to progressively make changes further and further down the execution graph until you reach the final node.

Our first issue is the following error:.

According to recent reports, luckily this error gives us quite a bit of information. We can look at the VisionRotaryEmbedding layer and see the following code:.

Although torch.arange has a dtype argument, coremltools ignores this for arange and always outputs int32. We can simply add a cast after the arange to fix this issue, commit here.

After fixing this, running the conversion again leads us to our next glitch at repeat_interleave:.

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:.

cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It's derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call, commit here.

Industry observers note that onto the next! This time, we get a more cryptic error:.

This is again due to the masking logic to handle variable length sequences. Since we are only processing a single image (not a video or batch of images), we don't really need attention masking at all! Therefore, we can just use a mask of all True. To prepare ourselves for the Neural Engine conversion, we also switch from using a boolean mask to a float mask of all zeros, as the Neural Engine does not support bool tensors commit here.

Industry observers note that with all of this done, the model should now successfully convert to CoreML! However, when we run the model, we get the following error:.

This reshape could be in multiple places! Luckily, we can use a previous warning message to help us track down the issue:.

Most ML compilers do not like dynamic control flow. Luckily for us, as we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove the loop and process the single h, w pair, commit here.

And there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:.

According to recent reports, now that we've got the model working, let's evaluate the size and performance. The good news is the model is working, the bad news is that it's over 5GB! This is completely untenable for on device deployment! To benchmark the computation time, we can use the built in XCode tooling by calling:.

which will launch the XCode inspector for the model. After clicking + Performance Report and launching a report on all compute devices, you should see something like the following:.

Over a second for a single forward pass of the vision encoder! We have lots of more work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for those looking to ditch cloud storage this Black Friday, UGreen's DXP4800 GT 4-bay NAS enclosure has gone on sale with a lovely 20% discount at Amazon, marking the second time it's returned to its all-time low price point. While you'll have to bring your own drives, the system is packed full of functionality and offers solid specifications, which make it ideal for any backups or while acting as a small home server. Moreover, this model has an upgraded processor compared to its predecessor (which is currently more expensive), and the DXP4800 GT also has 10GbE for rapid file transfers whenever you need it.

In terms of specifications, the UGreen DXP4800 GT sports an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with four cores and eight threads, running at 3.7 GHz, with 8GB of onboard DDR4 memory and support for up to 64GB for those looking to upgrade. The system drive offers 64GB of eMMC, but can be switched over to one of the two m.2 NVMe drive slots, and dual 10GbE connectors. Of course, you also get a total of four drive bays, supporting HDDs of up to 32 TB in size. When maxed out across all bays and drives, you pack up to 144TB of storage in total. You can also use two of the bays for 2.5-inch SATA drives or U.2 NVMe drives.

The UGreen DXP4800 GT can support a total of 144 TB of storage across its 4 drive bays and 2 NVMe slots. The enclosure runs an AMD Ryzen Embedded CPU with 8GB of DDR4 memory and 64GB of eMMC system storage. Expect support for RAID 0 / 1 / 5 / 6 / 10 / JBOD and Basic, shipping with UGOS.

Industry observers note that UGreen's NAS systems ship with their own proprietary OS, named UGOS Pro. However, since it's a typical x86-based machine, you should be able to get TrueNAS or Unraid up and running with some tinkering; however, attempting this would void the device's 2-year limited warranty. So before you buy, do some research and see whether or not UGOS Pro is for you before committing completely.

Out of the box, the system supports a host of RAID configurations: 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, JBOD, and Basic. For those looking for connectivity, you should expect a SD 3.0 slot on the front, with a total of 2 USB-A (3.2 Gen 2), 2 USB-A (2.0), and 1 USB-C (3.2 Gen 2) ports in total which should suit many owners.

Purchasing a NAS this Black Friday doesn't have to be expensive, so if UGreen's DXP4800 GT suits your home backup or server needs, it's difficult to argue with the offer price, where you can save $132 on the device at Amazon right now.

Breaking: BigCodeArena: Judging code generations end to end with code executions

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult.
  • Industry observers note that inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces.
  • The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult. While humans can easily spot whether a piece of code "looks right," determining if it actually works correctly, handles edge cases properly, and produces the intended result requires running and testing it. This is why today, we're thrilled to announce BigCodeArena -- the first human-in-the-loop platform for evaluating code generation models through execution.

Industry observers note that inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces. Just submit a coding task, watch two different models generate solutions, execute both programs, and vote on which model produced better results. The outcomes are organized into a leaderboard that displays the community's highest-rated models.

The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods. Traditional benchmarks like HumanEval test code against predefined test cases, but these represent only a tiny fraction of real-world programming tasks. Human evaluation platforms exist for general chatbots, but they fall short for code: reading raw source code and mentally simulating its execution is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially for longer programs or complex UI applications.

Sources indicate that you ask two AI models to build a responsive photo gallery website. Both generate code that looks syntactically correct. But which one is actually better? Without running the code, it's nearly impossible to tell. One might produce a beautiful, functional grid layout, while the other might have subtle bugs or poor styling that only become apparent when rendered in a browser.

This observation led us to a key insight: execution feedback is essential for humans to judge code quality reliably. That's exactly what BigCodeArena provides.

BigCodeArena extends the Chatbot Arena framework with powerful features specifically designed for code evaluation:.

Sources indicate that every code snippet generated by models is automatically executed in isolated sandbox environments. Whether it's a Python script, a React web app, a PyGame game, or a C++ algorithm, you can see the actual output, not just the source code.

We currently support 10 languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, C, C++, Java, Go, Rust, and Markdown) and 8 execution environments:.

Unlike static code comparison, you can actually interact with the generated applications:.

Recent findings suggest that real programming isn't one-and-done. BigCodeArena supports multi-turn interactions, allowing you to refine requirements, ask for features to be added, or request bug fixes -- just like working with a real coding assistant.

Since launching in February 2025, BigCodeArena has collected over 14,000 conversations from more than 500 unique users, with 4,700+ high-quality preference votes comparing 10 frontier LLMs.

Our users have explored remarkably diverse coding scenarios:.

Python dominates with over 4,000 conversations, followed by JavaScript/TypeScript (3,359), HTML (1,601), and C++ (642). Among frameworks, direct Python interpreters lead usage (6,000 sessions), with React (2,729), Core Web (1,574), Streamlit (1,254), and PyGame (1,087) also seeing heavy use.

Industry observers note that most interactions are focused and efficient: 76% of conversations consist of just 2 turns (one request, one response), with a mean conversation length of 4.12 messages. However, the platform supports extended multi-turn debugging sessions when needed, with some conversations exceeding 10 turns as users refine complex applications.

Sources indicate that from our 14K conversations, we filtered for high-quality pairwise comparisons: conversations with at least two turns and actual code execution. This yielded 4,731 voting samples, with each evaluated model receiving at least 700 votes. We aggregate these votes into Elo ratings using the Bradley-Terry model, which estimates the probability that one model beats another based on head-to-head comparisons.

To ensure robust rankings, we use 100 bootstrap resamples to construct 95% confidence intervals, so we can identify statistically significant performance differences between models.

We evaluate models under three settings to control for different factors:.

Rankings remain remarkably consistent across all three settings, revealing clear performance tiers:.

Recent findings suggest that top Tier: o3-mini and o1-mini consistently lead with the highest Elo ratings and tight confidence intervals. These models maintain top performance regardless of environment or language constraints, showing strong robustness across coding scenarios. Claude-3.5-Sonnet follows closely, particularly excelling when language is controlled.

In a recent development, mid Tier: GPT-4o, o1, and Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash form a competitive middle tier. GPT-4o demonstrates some sensitivity to language matching, suggesting room for improvement in multilingual consistency.

Open Source Models: Qwen2.5 variants and Llama-3.3-70B lag behind frontier proprietary models, highlighting the performance gap that remains between leading closed and open models.

According to recent reports, figure: Overall win rate heatmaps (percentage of all pairwise comparisons won) of each model in the sessions across languages (left) and execution environments (right). For each category, we only keep models that appear in at least 3 conversation sessions.

Breaking down performance by programming language reveals interesting patterns:.

Analyzing win rates by execution environment reveals how models handle different runtime contexts:.

Robust Performers: o3-mini maintains consistently strong performance across React, Streamlit, Gradio, Core Web, and PyGame, demonstrating excellent environmental adaptability.

Stable but Selective: Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.0-Flash show generally stable performance but with reduced win rates in complex UI-heavy environments like Vue and Mermaid.

Industry observers note that framework-Specific Weaknesses: Qwen2.5 models, while competitive in some web frameworks (Core Web, React), struggle significantly with interactive and visualization-oriented environments like PyGame, Vue, and Mermaid. These environments often require precise handling of control flow, graphics rendering, and package dependencies.

These results highlight an important insight: aggregate Elo scores don't tell the whole story. Some models remain brittle under specific runtime constraints, and execution environment matters significantly for real-world deployment.

To advance research beyond crowdsourced evaluation, we're releasing two complementary benchmarks:.

Building on our 4,700+ preference votes, BigCodeReward tests how well LLMs can judge code quality when acting as reward models. The key finding? Execution results dramatically improve judgment accuracy.

When models can see execution outputs (screenshots of web apps, game visuals, program logs), their alignment with human preferences increases substantially:.

This reinforces our core thesis: you can't reliably judge code without running it -- and this applies to both humans and AI judges.

Inspired by Arena-Hard-Auto, AutoCodeArena provides a scalable way to evaluate upcoming models without waiting for thousands of human votes. We carefully selected 600 representative prompts from our crowdsourced data, spanning all programming topics and frameworks.

Using automated LLM judges (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) to evaluate code execution results against a GPT-4.1 baseline, we can rapidly benchmark new models. This approach enables weekly leaderboard updates as new models are released.

Our automated benchmark evaluated 20+ cutting-edge models, including recently released systems:.

It has been revealed that figure: Win rates of recent LLMs on AutoCodeArena against a GPT-4.1 baseline, judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The 50% mark represents parity with GPT-4.1. Models above this line outperform the baseline, while those below underperform. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Note: Claude-3.7-Sonnet is excluded from rankings to avoid self-judgment bias, and GPT-4.1 appears only as the reference baseline.

The results show that while proprietary models maintain an edge, open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, with some approaching GPT-4.1-level performance.

Whether you're building a React dashboard, creating a PyGame game, solving algorithmic challenges, or generating creative visualizations, BigCodeArena lets you see which models truly deliver.

Recent findings suggest that evaluating code isn't like evaluating text -- you need to run it, test it, and interact with it. BigCodeArena makes this possible at scale, combining human judgment with real execution feedback to create the most reliable evaluation platform for code generation models.
