AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Industry observers note that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

Recent findings suggest that • Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

Recent findings suggest that • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it claims it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Recent findings suggest that limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your proposal. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

Recent findings suggest that GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Industry observers note that strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The firm’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and proposal prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Industry observers note that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, states very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

It has been revealed that turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

In a recent development, strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

It has been revealed that sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

It has been revealed that strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page claims false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

In a recent development, the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Industry observers note that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

Sources indicate that • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. Latest models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

Sources indicate that • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

Sources indicate that openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Recent findings suggest that most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

In a recent development, • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

It has been revealed that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and revision as newly introduced models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

According to recent reports, • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Industry observers note that because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

Recent findings suggest that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

Recent findings suggest that • Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

Sources indicate that • Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

It has been revealed that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

It has been revealed that when using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

In practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A compound AI approach to Indian personas grounded in real-world distributions.

India represents one of the world's largest AI opportunities — with over 700 million internet users, a multitude of languages, and a rapidly growing developer ecosystem. Yet, most open datasets reflect Western norms and English-only contexts, creating a data gap that limits AI adoption in India's multilingual, multi-script environment.

Today, we're releasing Nemotron-Personas-India, the first open synthetic dataset of Indic personas aligned to India's real-world demographic, geographic, and cultural distributions. Licensed under CC BY 4.0, this dataset offers a privacy-preserving, regulation-ready foundation for scaling AI systems that reflect Indian society—without relying on sensitive personal data.

Industry observers note that built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's enterprise-grade synthetic data generation microservice, Nemotron-Personas-India extends our global collection of Sovereign AI datasets. It builds on the success of our US and Japan persona datasets and includes upcoming features designed specifically for India's culturally rich landscape.

This dataset integrates seamlessly with Nemotron models and other open-source LLMs, making it easy to fine-tune AI systems for Indian use cases—from multilingual chatbots to culturally-grounded specialized copilots.

This release complements our earlier suite of Hindi evaluation datasets — including ChatRAG-Hi, IFEval-Hi, MT-Bench-Hi, GSM8K-Hi, and BFCL-Hi — supporting a complete pipeline from synthetic data generation to rigorous model evaluation for Indian AI systems.

In a recent development, produced using NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's microservice for synthetic data generation. This compound AI system enables generation with complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and supports multiple generation backends – the necessary tooling to scale a synthetic dataset of this size. We also leveraged the following models:.

This dataset was aligned to India’s official demographic distributions from the 2011 Census and expanded to include attributes essential for trustworthy AI training:.

No real names. No re-identification risk.

Industry observers note that all personas are fully synthetic. While grounded in real-world distributions from the 2011 Census and Parsed Indian Electoral Rolls data, no data is tied to any living or deceased individual. This ensures developers can safely train AI systems without privacy risks or regulatory barriers.

Built for India, Ready for the World.

Nemotron‑Personas‑India is designed for developers building Sovereign AI systems for the Indian market, as well as global teams looking to adapt models to India’s unique linguistic, cultural, and social context.

Most open datasets today reflect English-speaking, Western norms—limiting AI performance in India’s multilingual, multi-script, and demographically complex environments.

With Nemotron‑Personas‑India, teams can:.

Industry observers note that india's 1.4 billion people speak hundreds of languages and live across vast cultural, economic, and geographic divides. India's National AI Portal estimates over 7,000 AI startups and research institutions are working to build locally relevant AI systems, and the Digital India initiative and government programs like IndiaAI are accelerating adoption.

But progress is constrained by a fundamental gap: high-quality, culturally grounded training data that reflects India's demographic reality. Without representative datasets, AI systems struggle with code-switching between English and Hindi, fail to understand regional occupational categories, and miss cultural context essential for trust and adoption.

The dataset improves diversity of synthetically-generated data, mitigates biases, and prevents model collapse (degradation caused by uncurated training on another model's outputs) by reflecting India's real geographic and demographic distributions.

Nemotron-Personas-India supports Indian model builders in developing Sovereign AI systems that incorporate crucial region-specific demographics and cultural context.

Want to build AI systems that understand India's culture, languages, and people?

Whether you're an Indian model builder developing Sovereign AI or a global developer seeking better regional adoption, Nemotron-Personas-India provides the authentic, privacy-safe foundation your applications need.

According to recent reports, download it. Fine-tune it. Build AI that understands India. If you’re ready to go deeper, an extended version of Nemotron-Personas-India (which includes e.g., first/last names, religion, and synthetic addresses) is available in NeMo Data Designer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with the growing capability of large language models (LLMs), a latest class of models has emerged: Vision Language Models (VLMs). These models can analyze images and videos to describe scenes, create captions, and answer questions about visual content.

Sources indicate that while running AI models on your own device can be difficult as these models are often computationally demanding, it also offers significant benefits: including improved privacy since your data stays on your machine, and enhanced speed and reliability because you're not dependent on an internet connection or external servers. This is where tools like Optimum Intel and OpenVINO come in, along with a small, efficient model like SmolVLM. In this blog post, we'll walk you through three easy steps to get a VLM running locally, with no expensive hardware or GPUs required (though you can run all the code samples from this blog post on Intel GPUs).

It has been revealed that small models like SmolVLM are built for low-resource consumption, but they can be further optimized. In this blog post we will see how to optimize your model, to lower memory usage and speedup inference, making it more efficient for deployment on devices with limited resources.

To follow this tutorial, you need to install optimum and openvino, which you can do with:.

First, you will need to convert your model to the OpenVINO IR. There are multiple options to do it:.

Now it’s time to optimize your model. Quantization reduces the precision of the model weights and/or activations, leading to smaller, faster models. Essentially, it's a way to map values from a high-precision data type, such as 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32), to a lower-precision format, typically 8-bit integers (INT8). While this process offers several key benefits, it can also impact in a potential loss of accuracy.

Optimum supports two main post-training quantization methods:.

Recent findings suggest that weight-only quantization means that only the weights are quantized but activations remain in their original precisions. As a result, the model becomes smaller and more memory-efficient, improving loading times. But since activations are not quantized, inference speed gains are limited. Weight-only quantization is a simple first step since it usually doesn’t result in significant accuracy degradation.

Since OpenVINO 2024.3, if the model's weight have been quantized, the corresponding activations will also be quantized at runtime, leading to additional speedup depending on the device.

In order to run it, you will need to create a quantization configuration OVWeightQuantizationConfig as follows:.

With Static Quantization, both weights and activations are quantized before inference. To achieve the best estimate for the activation quantization parameters, we perform a calibration step. During this step, a small representative dataset is fed through the model. In our case, we will use 50 samples of the contextual dataset and will apply static quantization on the vision encoder while weight-only quantization will be applied on the rest of the model. Experiments show that applying static quantization on the vision encoder provides a noticeable performance improvement without significant accuracy degradation. Since the vision encoder is called only once per generation, the overall performance gain from applying static quantization on this component is lower than the gain achieved by optimizing more frequently used components like the language model. Nevertheless, this approach can be beneficial in certain scenarios. For example, when short answers are needed, especially with multiple images as input.

Sources indicate that quantizing activations adds small errors that can build up and affect accuracy, so careful testing afterward is key. More information and examples can be found in our documentation.

You can now run inference with your quantized model:.

If you have a recent Intel laptop, Intel AI PC, or Intel discrete GPU, you can load the model on GPU by adding device="gpu" when loading your model:.

We also created a space so you can play with the original model and its quantized variants obtained by respectively applying weight-only quantization and mixed quantization. This demo runs on 4th Generation Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) processors.

To reproduce our results, check out our notebook.

We ran a benchmark to compare the performance of the PyTorch, OpenVINO, and OpenVINO 8-bit WOQ versions of the original model. The goal was to evaluate the impact of weight-only quantization on latency and throughput on Intel CPU hardware. For this test, we used a single image as input.

We measured the following metrics to evaluate the model's performance:.

Here are the results on Intel CPU:.

This benchmark demonstrates how small, optimized multimodal models, like SmolVLM2-256M, perform on Intel CPUs across different configurations. According to the tests, the PyTorch version indicates high latency, with a time to first token (TTFT) of over 5s with a decoding throughput of 0.7 tokens/s. Simply converting the model with Optimum and running it on OpenVINO drastically reduces the time to first token (TTFT) to 0.42s (x12 speedup) and raises throughput to 47 tokens/s (x65). Applying 8-bit weight-only quantization further reduces TTFT (x1.7) and increases throughput (x1.4), while also reducing model size and improving efficiency.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, when one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and shows which setting to change for your app.

Industry observers note that I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Every server got the same requests:.

Industry observers note that ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

Sources indicate that the tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code claims so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next shows.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

The obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

The cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ indicates the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

That context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps showed 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

Recent findings suggest that LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:.

The price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

Industry observers note that in Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

Recent findings suggest that the last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many owners, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

All figures are total tokens per second.

Recent findings suggest that with its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds upcoming requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:.

According to recent reports, for a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:.

Industry observers note that if you run an older llama.cpp, update first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a latest CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

It reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:.

According to recent reports, setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

It starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

Sources indicate that it also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

It has been revealed that all four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:.

Industry observers note that in Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:.

Industry observers note that qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

It has been revealed that none of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

It has been revealed that before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your users' wait more than the choice of engine.

Sources indicate that not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Recent findings suggest that ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

When many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

Sources indicate that usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight.
  • They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules.
  • Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

Sources indicate that if the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a plan, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to demonstrate the real-world value of upgrading to Google’s latest C4 Virtual Machine (VM) running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors (codenamed Granite Rapids (GNR)). According to recent reports, the results are in, and they are impressive, demonstrating a 1.7x improvement in Total Cost of Ownership(TCO) over the previous-generation Google C3 VM instances. The Google Cloud C4 VM instance further resulted in:.

GPT OSS is a common name for an open-source Mixture of Experts (MoE) model released by OpenAI. An MoE model is a deep neural network architecture that uses specialized “expert” sub-networks and a “gating network” to decide which experts to use for a given input. MoE models allow you to scale your model capacity efficiently without linearly scaling compute costs. They also allow for specialization, where different “experts” learn different skills, allowing them to adapt to diverse data distributions.

Even with very large parameters, only a small subset of experts is activated per token, making CPU inference viable.

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to merge an expert execution optimization (PR #40304) to eliminate redundant computation where every expert processed all tokens to transformers. This optimization directed each expert to run only on the tokens it is routed to, removing FLOPs waste and improving utilization.

Industry observers note that we benchmarked GPT OSS under a controlled, repeatable generation workload to isolate architectural differences (GCP C4 VMs on Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) vs GCP C3 VMs on 4th Gen Intel Xeon Processors (SPR)) and MoE execution efficiency. The focus is steady‑state decoding (per‑token latency) and end‑to‑end normalized throughput with increasing batch size while keeping sequence lengths fixed. All runs use static KV cache and SDPA attention for determinism.

Industry observers note that DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

Runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

The catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the newly introduced reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

AI for Food Allergies

📅 16 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that let’s get straight to the point: worldwide, an estimated 220 million people suffer from at least one food allergy, and in the United States alone, this accounts for roughly 10% of the population.
  • Industry observers note that in recent years, biomedical research has made several remarkable advances: from experimental vaccines and desensitization-based immunotherapies to improved diagnostic tools capable of identifying specific allergen sensitivities with unprecedented precision.
  • In a recent development, in the meantime, we’ve also witnessed groundbreaking progress in artificial intelligence applied to biology and medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that let’s get straight to the point: worldwide, an estimated 220 million people suffer from at least one food allergy, and in the United States alone, this accounts for roughly 10% of the population. This means that if you don’t have an allergy, you’ll likely know someone who does — and it’s not a pleasant situation to be in. This condition affects not only patients’ physical health but also takes a significant toll on their mental well-being and overall quality of life.

Industry observers note that in recent years, biomedical research has made several remarkable advances: from experimental vaccines and desensitization-based immunotherapies to improved diagnostic tools capable of identifying specific allergen sensitivities with unprecedented precision. These developments are pointing us in the right direction toward building long-term immune tolerance, but we’re not quite there yet.

In a recent development, in the meantime, we’ve also witnessed groundbreaking progress in artificial intelligence applied to biology and medicine. Models like AlphaFold and Boltz-1 have revolutionized protein structure prediction, while AI-driven approaches in genomics, drug discovery, and molecular modeling are accelerating the pace of biomedical innovation. The convergence of these worlds is opening up upcoming possibilities for understanding, predicting, and ultimately treating complex immune conditions such as food allergies.

It has been revealed that four among the major allergenic proteins folded by AlphaFold. Up left to bottom right: glycinin (soybean), ovalbumin (egg), alpha lactalbumin (milk), ara-h-2 (peanut).

It has been revealed that our vision with the AI for Food Allergies project is to build the first community-driven research lab dedicated to exploring how artificial intelligence can meaningfully advance the field of food allergy research. We aim to bridge the gap between cutting-edge AI and biomedical science by developing open, collaborative projects that contribute tangible value to researchers, clinicians, and patients alike.

The last couple of years have been transformative for food allergy research. Artificial intelligence, once limited to image recognition or text translation, now operates comfortably in the biological and regulatory spaces that define food safety.

This evolution began with early bioinformatics techniques utilized sequence alignment and physicochemical descriptors to detect and flag potential allergens. Databases such as SDAP and AllergenOnline were used to identify cross-reactive proteins. Machine-learning algorithms such as AllerHunter, and NetAllergen later enhanced these methods, training on thousands of known allergens and non-allergens to improve predictive accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that today, at the molecular level, deep learning models like ProtBERT, ESM-2, and AllergenBERT can analyze amino-acid sequences to predict whether a protein might act as an allergen. They identify subtle biochemical patterns, sequence motifs, secondary-structure signals, and epitope similarities, which correlate with immune reactions. For example, AllergenAI applies convolutional neural networks to allergen sequences from SDAP 2.0, COMPARE, and AlgPred 2, uncovering motifs essential for IgE binding and demonstrating the promise of integrating structural data into prediction pipelines What used to require months of lab experiments can now be screened computationally, dramatically accelerating allergen discovery in novel foods and plant-based proteins.

Industry observers note that concurrently, AI is expanding the scope of allergy therapeutics through advances in drug-target interaction (DTI) modelling. Deep neural networks, graph neural networks and transformer models utilize data from chemogenomic datasets such as DAVIS, PDBbind to predict binding affinities, enabling virtual screening of compounds that can potentially inhibit IgE–FcεRI binding or modulate inflammatory pathways. Multimodal datasets that contain molecular structures, transcriptomics and imaging readouts can be utilized for tasks such as small molecule generation, prediction of properties and assessment of immune cell response. The subsequent subheadings present critical datasets supporting the mentioned AI approaches and explain how each resource is employed in food allergy drug design.

Industry observers note that in clinical research, AI is helping refine diagnostics. Traditionally, allergists rely on a mix of skin-prick results, serum-specific IgE levels, and patient history, but interpreting these together is difficult. Machine learning models have begun combining these modalities to estimate the true probability of a food allergy, reducing unnecessary oral food challenges and improving patient safety. Importantly, these models don’t replace doctors, they simply reduce uncertainty and provide interpretable probabilities rather than binary outcomes.

According to recent reports, on the consumer and regulatory side, advances in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV) have made it possible to read and understand ingredient labels at scale. NLP models trained on multilingual data can detect hidden or misspelled allergen names (“tahini” → sesame, “paneer” → dairy), while vision models can read curved, low-light packaging and extract ingredient text more reliably than standard OCR systems. Combined with live monitoring of FDA and USDA recall feeds, AI can now alert consumers to undeclared allergen risks in near real time.

Industry observers note that A fundamental step in applying Machine Learning to this field is having access to high-quality data. As highlighted by Channing and Ghosh in their position paper “AI for Scientific Discovery is a Social Problem”, the real challenge in ML for science goes beyond advanced models and powerful GPUs. It lies in the scarcity, fragmentation, and inaccessibility of data. This glitch is particularly evident in the biomedical domain, where data gatekeeping, inconsistent standards, and lack of interoperability often hinder collaboration and slows down progress.

Industry observers note that the first milestone of our community is dedicated to addressing this very challenge. We have curated Awesome Food Allergy Datasets, the first open collection of datasets on food allergies, meticulously annotated and categorized to serve as a foundation for future research. By making this resource openly accessible, we aim to accelerate discovery, foster collaboration, and lower the entry barrier for researchers and innovators interested in applying AI to this critical field.

Stats about the distribution of our datasets by data type, category and public availability.

We organize this resource into three complementary layers, each designed to serve a specific part of the AI-for-Food-Allergies ecosystem.

At the molecular level, we are assembling what may become the most complete open dataset for allergen and protein analysis ever built. It merges classical allergen repositories with next-generation molecular and drug-target databases, enabling deep learning models to move seamlessly from sequence to structure to immune response.

According to recent reports, this layer draws from trusted allergen-focused sources such as WHO/IUIS Allergen Nomenclature Database, AllergenOnline, Allergen30,AllerBase, AllFam, Allermatch, AllerHunter, AllerCatPro 2.0, AllergenAI,NetAllergen, AllerTOP v1.1, Alleropedia, Allergome, and the Allergen Family Database. These provide verified allergenic and non-allergenic protein sequences, family classifications, and cross-reactivity annotations.

In a recent development, to capture the biochemical and structural side of allergenicity, we integrate resources like SDAP 2.0, PDBBind+, ProPepper, and quantum-chemistry datasets including nabla²DFT, QM, QDπ, QCML, and QCDGE. These datasets provide molecular surfaces, binding affinities, and electrostatic descriptors that help AI models learn why certain proteins interact with IgE antibodies.

Because allergic response often overlaps with pharmacology, this layer also incorporates drug–target and compound databases such as DAVIS, QSAR, e-Drug3D, Stanford Drug Data, DrugCentral, MedKG, Therapeutic Target Database, STITCH, Probes & Drugs, IUPHAR Pharmacology, and Enamine REAL. These enable studies of cross-reactivity between allergens and drugs, side-effects that mimic allergic reactions, and opportunities for immunomodulatory therapy.

According to recent reports, each record in this unified dataset is annotated with sequence data, taxonomy, molecular descriptors, and literature references. We apply homology reduction to prevent data leakage between training and test sets and evaluate model quality using AUROC, AUPRC, MCC, and calibration scores. This layer serves as the foundation for building transformer-based models that predict allergenicity, drug–allergen interactions, and cross-reactive epitopes.

Recent findings suggest that allergies begin at the immune level, and understanding that requires human data. The second layer combines immunology, clinical, and trial datasets to help researchers model how allergic sensitization, tolerance, and treatment evolve over time.

From the immunological perspective, we include the IEDB (Immune Epitope Database) and its Analysis Resource, alongside specialized datasets like AlgPred 2.0, Allergen30, Allergen Peptide Browser, and ProPepper, which map B- and T-cell epitopes and antibody binding regions.

For studying patient-level outcomes, we integrate clinical and population datasets such as Food Anaphylaxis ML Dataset (TIP), Food Allergy Risk Stratification Dataset, Food Allergy & Intolerance Dataset, and AllergyMap. Large-scale cohorts like HealthNuts, CHILD, and DIABIMMUNE, plus microbiome-focused datasets (e.g., Dysfunctional Gut Microbiome Networks in Childhood IgE-Mediated Food Allergy and Akkermansia muciniphila in Fibre-Deprived Mice), enrich this layer with genetic and microbial context.

Simulated datasets — such as the Simulated Allergen Immunotherapy Trials Dataset, Simulated AIT Trials Dataset, and FARE Food Allergy Research data — allow us to model the long-term response to desensitization therapies without exposing patients to risk.

It has been revealed that genetic and biochemical variability is represented through GWAS, DNA Methylation GSE59999, and the Human Metabolome Database. These allow multi-omics studies of how genes, metabolism, and environment combine to shape allergic disease.

Together, these resources form the backbone for predictive models that estimate reaction risk, identify candidate biomarkers, and simulate therapy outcomes — a foundation for safer, more personalized allergy care.

Recent findings suggest that the final layer connects lab science to real-world food safety. Here, we focus on datasets that describe what consumers actually eat, how products are labeled, and how authorities respond to allergen incidents.

According to recent reports, we curate large multilingual ingredient and product databases such as Open Food Facts, Food Ingredients and Allergens, Ingredients with 16 Allergen Tags, Allergen Status of Food Products, and FSA Allergen Database Service (UK Nut Allergy Registry). Complementary regulatory datasets include Swiss Legislation on Food Allergens, COMPARE, and the FSA Allergen Database Service, which provide consistent allergen codes and labeling standards.

For real-world adverse-event tracking, we rely on CAERS (CFSAN Adverse Event Reporting System), PEAR – Partners’ Enterprise-wide Allergy Repository, and Food: Allergen and Allergy, which capture anonymized clinical reports and recall histories. Government recall sources from FDA, USDA, and CFIA, as well as global registries, are continuously ingested to monitor undeclared-allergen events and labeling failures.

Recent findings suggest that these datasets feed into our Multilingual Ingredient and Label Corpus, where text data are normalized through an ontology that maps local terms (“tahini,” “gingelly,” “sesame paste”) to canonical allergens. Synthetic label images are generated to mimic supermarket conditions — glare, blur, curved surfaces, and multi-language fonts — allowing models to learn in realistic settings.

By combining structured recall data with visual and linguistic information, this layer empowers AI systems that can read packaging, understand its content, and flag inconsistencies in real time.

Our collection is available through our dedicated Hugging Face datasets repository. You can explore it interactively using the hf space we've developed, which features name-based search along with convenient filtering options by category, task, and data type.

In a recent development, we welcome contributions! Our datasets list is maintained on a dedicated GitHub repository where you can submit pull requests to help us grow the collection.

In a recent development, this first work is a testament on the fact that community-driven open science not only is possible, but is a great idea. Take our case: in just a few weeks, more than 20 contributors from different backgrounds came together working on a food allergy related project. This reveals how even a specialized scientific topic perceived as nieche can spark geniune interest and momentum.

It’s our 0-to-1 moment: proof that when people unite around a clear purpose, even a small initiative can grow into something transformative. And who knows — maybe one day, food allergy research will have its own AlphaFold moment.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, our focus will shift toward hands-on, scientifically meaningful projects that build on this foundation. Guided by scientific advisors and domain experts, we aim to foster collaborative, community-driven research that advances the science of food allergies.

Our goal is to harness the power of AI to tackle key scientific questions, such as:.

Whether you’re a researcher, student, developer, or simply passionate about open science, we’d love to have you join us.
