#103506. Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2034 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • Industry observers note that today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

Industry observers note that today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

Industry observers note that this growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

Sources indicate that for v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

The first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each newly introduced model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

It has been revealed that transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 fresh models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

In a recent development, over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

It has been revealed that we give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

While we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for new model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

We’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a fresh model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

Industry observers note that we’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

It has been revealed that we'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

With its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

-- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a substantial focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

Sources indicate that we continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, new APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

In a recent development, similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two fresh APIs dedicated to inference:.

It has been revealed that we see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

The Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more consumers. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

It has been revealed that standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

In a recent development, we've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

Recent findings suggest that the Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

It’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

According to recent reports, finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Quantization is quickly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

We're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate new quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

Industry observers note that the overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

Version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

In a recent development, we took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Industry observers note that now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

Awesome work, great job of maintaining the library, it sure isn't easy with all the different architectures and advancements.

Congratulations for the launch !

No, you don’t! It’s just pure control. Researchers would love to have direct PyTorch only access to the architecture, training, and inference code for different models without this Transformers blab.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Moon is now a few days past its First Quarter phase, and we're well into the Waxing Gibbous stage, which means each night, a little more of its surface is illuminated. This pattern will continue until we reach the Full Moon.

As of Friday, Nov. 20, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 77% of its surface visible.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis and Tranquillitatis, as well as the Kepler Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Posidonius Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 14, and 17 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

Industry observers note that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a Upcoming Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

Sources indicate that first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Breaking: We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial shows you how it works and how to use it yourself.

Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

According to recent reports, hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

Let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

In a recent development, the coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

Industry observers note that the open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

This works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

Industry observers note that this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

It has been revealed that that's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

Industry observers note that the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

Recent findings suggest that SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

Use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

For models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

Sources indicate that DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and indicates you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

You can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

It has been revealed that the model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

Sources indicate that for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train swiftly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

For small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

Industry observers note that for medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

It has been revealed that always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Sources indicate that dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

Recent findings suggest that real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

Sources indicate that this demonstrates training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

Recent findings suggest that if something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

Recent findings suggest that after training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

We've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

The skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

Temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

We benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

Industry observers note that we compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and demonstrates the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

DeepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Recent findings suggest that check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

Industry observers note that executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

#103500. Latest Update: Pre-Fill Your Skipped Slots. Just Don't Believe What They Say.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1252 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Pre-Fill Your Skipped Slots. Just Don't Believe What They Say.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that 271 milliseconds.
  • In a recent development, johnnylemonny asked about this in the comments on his Promise.all piece, and his question was sharper than most of the replies it got.
  • In a recent development, the setup was small on purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that 271 milliseconds. That is how long my batch lived before task 4 threw, and it is the only number in this piece that came out the same no matter what I did to the results array. Everything else about the abort changed depending on one small decision made before the first worker started: whether the results array was full of holes, or full of slots marked skipped.

In a recent development, johnnylemonny asked about this in the comments on his Promise.all piece, and his question was sharper than most of the replies it got. In a fail-fast mapWithConcurrency, rethrowing inside the worker makes the whole call reject, so the results array is never returned and the slots that never started stay uninitialized holes. His fix: fill the array with { status: "skipped" } before starting the workers, so the caller can tell the tasks that failed apart from the ones that never ran. I ran his shape twice, both ways, and he is right about the shape and wrong about one slot. The pre-fill fixes the array. It does not fix what the array notes about the task that threw.

In a recent development, the setup was small on purpose. Ten tasks, three workers, one throw. Each task waits a set time and then returns { status: "ok", value: i * 10 }, except task 4, which throws after 150 milliseconds. The delays were picked so the throw lands mid-batch: tasks 0, 1 and 2 start first, task 4 starts once task 0 finishes, and it throws at 270 milliseconds, with five tasks still waiting or running. Both arms ran twice, and both repeats came back identical down to the tenth of a millisecond, so the numbers below are the run, not an average of two different ones.

The holes arm is worse than it looks in the code. results.length says 10, which is a lie in the only sense that matters: only 3 keys exist in the array. The other 7 slots are not undefined values. They are absence. Reading one gives you undefined, but asking whether it is there gives you false, and .map never even visits them: the callback ran 3 times out of 10. A consumer that counts finished work with .filter gets 3, which happens to be right, and a consumer that builds a report with .map gets a report with 3 entries and no complaint, which is wrong in a way nothing flags.

First, results[5].status throws a TypeError, because there is nothing at slot 5 to read a status from. Any consumer that reads a field off every slot crashes on the first hole it meets. Second, the holes do not survive a round-trip. JSON.stringify turns each hole into null, and after parsing, slot 4, the task that threw, and slot 5, a task that never started, are both null. A real null result, a failed task and a never-started task are now the same value, and no amount of reading the parsed data can separate them again. If the results ever cross a network boundary, get written to a file, or get logged as JSON, which is to say if they ever leave the function, the distinction johnnylemonny wanted is already gone.

The pre-filled arm reads like the answer. Ten keys, ten callbacks, no TypeError, no nulls after a round-trip. Slot 5 reads {"status":"skipped"}, which is true in the only sense the caller cares about: nothing ran there, nothing will, and the caller can retry it or report it without guessing. That is a real improvement, and it costs nothing measurable: the abort took 270.2 milliseconds against 271.1, a 0.9-millisecond gap across two identical repeats, which is timer noise, not a price.

But read slot 4. Task 4 is the one that threw. In the pre-filled array it reads {"status":"skipped"}, exactly like slot 5, which never started. It was not skipped. It ran, it hit a bad input row, and it failed. The pre-fill cannot tell those apart, because nothing ever wrote the failure down: the worker threw, the throw jumped out of the worker, and the slot kept whatever it was filled with at the start. Two more slots lie the same way. Slots 3 and 5 were still running when the abort landed at 271 milliseconds, their work abandoned halfway, and both read "skipped" too. Out of the seven slots marked skipped, only four never started. Two were mid-flight and one had failed, and the array calls all seven the same thing.

The fix for that is one line inside the worker, and it belongs in the same place as the pre-fill, not after it:.

With that, the failed slot reads failed, the never-started slots read skipped, and the in-flight ones still read skipped, which is the one remaining blur: a task that was running when everything stopped looks the same as a task that never began. Closing that last gap takes a "running" mark when the worker picks a task up, which is a second line and worth it only if your caller retries in-flight work differently from untouched work. For most callers, failed versus skipped is the distinction that decides the retry, and the pre-fill alone does not give it to you.

There is a catch underneath both arms, and it is the one that decides whether any of this matters. In the plain shape, Promise.all rejecting means the caller gets the error and nothing else. The results array is gone with the rejection. My run kept the array alive in a variable outside the call, which is how I could inspect it at all. A caller that just awaits the function gets an error object, and whether the array was holes or pre-filled skipped makes no difference to them, because they never see it.

Sources indicate that so the pre-fill is half a pattern. The other half is keeping the array reachable after the rejection: attach it to the error, return a partial result alongside it, or shape the call so the array comes back with the failure instead of being thrown away with it. Without that half, you have built a careful label for a box the caller never receives. With it, the pre-fill plus the failed-mark in the worker gives the caller everything it needs: three finished, one failed with its message attached, six never started, and no slot that has to be guessed at.

According to recent reports, that is where I land. Pre-fill the slots. It is one line, it costs nothing, and it turns an array the caller cannot read into one it can. Just do not stop there, and do not believe the labels it writes. Mark the failure in the worker before you rethrow, and make sure the array survives the rejection, or the pre-fill is a tidy label on a box nobody opens.

Have you hit this one in a real batch? What did your caller get back when the middle of the batch threw, and did it know which tasks were safe to retry?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially notable at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, remarked:.

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that your deploy script should only run if the tests pass. Your long build should tell you when it's done, so you stop checking the tab. And when you start a server, you want to know when it's actually ready, not just started.

You chain it: npm test && ./deploy.sh. Then you add ; say done at the end, and then || say failed, and the one line becomes a puzzle of &&, || and parentheses. For "ready", you watch the log until the line you're waiting for scrolls past.

With cmdbook, each of these has its own place on the command.

It has been revealed that 1. Pre: check first. Put npm test in the command's Pre field. It runs before the main command, in the same shell. If it fails, the main command is skipped, and the run demonstrates the test output.

2. Post: react to the result. Three fields, so you don't build the && / || yourself:.

Sources indicate that 3. Health check: know when it's ready. Tell cmdbook what "ready" means for this command: a port that accepts connections, a URL that returns 200, or a line in the output like Server started on port. While it runs, the command indicates running — healthy, or health check failed if it doesn't get there in time.

According to recent reports, your script stays the same. The checks and the notifications live next to it, not inside it.

All of this is in cmdbook's free blueprint.

Try cmdbook here: printf.app/cmdbook.

swift-huggingface implements a Python-compatible cache structure that allows seamless sharing between Swift and Python clients:.

The cache location follows the same environment variable conventions as Python:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Practical Claude, our guide series about Claude, reached KDP's series form on 17.11.2026 with no series description to paste.
  • Sources indicate that the KDP package carried the series title and the book's number, never the description.
  • Recent findings suggest that the change that shipped on 17.11.2026 in the new-Orqestra repository adds engine/kdp_series, a registry of series descriptions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Practical Claude, our guide series about Claude, reached KDP's series form on 17.11.2026 with no series description to paste. It was the fourth series in two months to stop there, after Exam Ready Study Guides (27.09), NeuraGrowth Little Coloring (04.10) and NeuraGrowth Little Dot Markers (25.10).

Sources indicate that the KDP package carried the series title and the book's number, never the description. The description lived in a vault note or in a file beside the package, so the person filling in the form had to go and find it.

Recent findings suggest that the change that shipped on 17.11.2026 in the new-Orqestra repository adds engine/kdp_series, a registry of series descriptions. It is stored as an AppSetting named kdp_series_registry, mapping series title to description, origin, date and first product. All four package builds now read it. It changed 8 files, with 662 lines added and 2 removed.

metadata.json now carries a series_kdp block with the title, Ordered or Unordered, the number, the description and the origin. When a series the registry does not know turns up as a first book, a model drafts the description. The record does not say more about how that draft is reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that the same day, rebuilding the package for book #225, a Claude book, raised a warning. Seven of its "Check it yourself" boxes cite Claude support pages whose last-changed date is 2026-11-17, the same day we read them. The alert states to check whether each change came before the read or after it, and the record here does not settle that.

If you publish books about a model's product pages, record the date you read each page, because a page that changes on that same day cannot tell you which version you read.

Originally published at neuragrowth.co. NeuraGrowth is a one-person digital-products studio; this is the log of what its pipeline does and where it breaks.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable for this scale yet. But stay tuned because we are working on it!

Nako Baev built THE OBJECT 01, a modular 3D-printed chair in recycled PETG that weighs 20 kg and pairs brutalist mass with Japanese restraint.

At 1.320 meters long and 0.875 meters tall, the lounge chair looks like poured concrete at first glance. Look closer at the studio shots and the surprise is its weight. Baev printed the entire structure from recycled PETG using a modular block system that keeps the frame down to 20 kg. It's heavy in presence, yet light enough to move across a room.

In a recent development, every joint follows a strict rectilinear block logic. In the wide studio view against the raw plastered wall, you can trace how four thick boxy volumes interlock to form the base, seat slab, cantilevered armrests, and tall backrest. Baev finished the 3D-printed chair in a cold grey tone he calls "Kyoto Fog." A close-up of his hand resting on the armrest reveals a smooth matte surface with crisp 90-degree edges, completely free of ornament or surface decoration.

In a recent development, the piece started as a few decisive lines on paper. Baev cites the quiet emptiness of raw architectural spaces, along with the lonely atmosphere of video games like Silent Hill and Half-Life, as key emotional references. An open monograph on the Bauhaus Building in Dessau sits beside him in the studio photos, echoing that interest in pure structural volume. To compress development time on this 3D-printed chair, he paired optimized printing workflows with AI tools for early form studies, technical testing, and final refinement.

Seen in use with Baev seated inside its deep frame, THE OBJECT 01 reads less like a prototype and more like usable architecture. It doesn't hide its geometry or its recycled material. Each modular block earns its place by cutting waste and holding the silhouette together.

Rackspace Spot Breach Exposes Kubernetes Secret Risks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on November 17 2026, threat actors gained initial access to Rackspace Spot by exploiting leaked service account credentials that had been exposed in a prior public repository.
  • According to recent reports, the malicious pods were instantiated under standard naming conventions that blended with legitimate workloads, allowing the operators to bypass basic monitoring thresholds.
  • Attackers systematically targeted secrets containing database credentials, API keys, and TLS certificates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on November 17 2026, threat actors gained initial access to Rackspace Spot by exploiting leaked service account credentials that had been exposed in a prior public repository. Within minutes of authentication, the attackers enumerated cluster resources across multiple customer environments and began deploying upcoming pods configured with elevated privileges.

According to recent reports, the malicious pods were instantiated under standard naming conventions that blended with legitimate workloads, allowing the operators to bypass basic monitoring thresholds. Once running, these containers mounted service account tokens and executed kubectl commands to list and retrieve secrets stored in customer namespaces.

Attackers systematically targeted secrets containing database credentials, API keys, and TLS certificates. They exfiltrated dozens of these objects per compromised cluster before any rate-limiting or anomaly detection triggered internal alerts. The rapid transition from credential use to secret access highlighted the absence of just-in-time permission boundaries within the Spot platform.

Forensic timelines later confirmed that the first secret read operations occurred less than eight minutes after the initial login, demonstrating how rapidly leaked credentials can translate into broad data exposure in Kubernetes environments lacking additional runtime controls.

Industry observers note that rackspace Spot functions as a managed Kubernetes platform that abstracts away infrastructure provisioning, letting teams deploy and scale container workloads through simplified APIs and integrated controls. This convenience, however, concentrates permissions in ways that expand the blast radius when credentials are misused.

Once attackers obtained valid access tokens, they operated with the same rights as legitimate users. The platform’s API surface allowed them to enumerate cluster nodes, inspect attached volumes, and traverse namespace configurations without triggering immediate alerts.

From that vantage point the attackers directly queried the Kubernetes Secrets store. These objects contained plaintext passwords for databases, service accounts, and external API keys that applications relied on for authentication and data access.

Managed platforms like Rackspace Spot therefore turn routine identity compromises into infrastructure-wide exposures. A single set of credentials can reveal both the physical layout of the cluster and the sensitive material required to move laterally or exfiltrate data.

Sources indicate that stolen Kubernetes Secrets containing database credentials immediately expose production data stores. An attacker who extracts a Secret holding PostgreSQL or MySQL connection strings can connect directly to the underlying RDS or Cloud SQL instance, bypassing network policies that only protect the cluster. The same Secrets often include API keys for internal services such as payment processors or logging platforms, allowing the intruder to enumerate additional resources and pivot across accounts without triggering standard perimeter alerts.

It has been revealed that service account tokens stored in Secrets compound the risk. These tokens frequently grant permissions to create pods or jobs in production namespaces, enabling attackers to spin up containers that mount the same persistent volumes or query the same etcd-backed resources used by legitimate workloads. Once inside, the attacker can harvest further Secrets from the cluster, expanding access to message queues, caches, and object storage buckets that hold customer data.

Sources indicate that manual reviews cannot detect these chained paths in real time. Security teams examining static manifests or occasional audit logs miss dynamic bindings that appear only at runtime, such as a Secret mounted into a newly scheduled pod or referenced by a cross-namespace RoleBinding. By the time an analyst traces the usage pattern, the attacker has already moved from the initial breach point into production databases and services.

Automated correlation of Secret access logs with workload identity graphs is required to surface these movements before damage occurs, as periodic human inspection simply lacks the speed and context to keep pace with Kubernetes' ephemeral nature.

Recent findings suggest that continuous compliance validation platforms run scheduled and event-driven scans across every Kubernetes cluster to surface exposed secrets and overly permissive RBAC bindings. These tools query the API server, etcd, and workload manifests in real time, flagging secrets stored in plain ConfigMaps or environment variables and roles that grant wildcard verbs on core resources. In the Rackspace Spot environment, such automated checks would have identified the same credential exposure paths that attackers later used to move laterally between customer namespaces.

Industry observers note that policy engines compare live cluster state against hardened baselines derived from CIS Kubernetes benchmarks and internal least-privilege requirements. When a scan detects a service account bound to cluster-admin or a secret mounted in a pod without encryption at rest, the finding is raised with remediation steps and risk scoring. This process closes the window between misconfiguration creation and exploitation that manual audits routinely miss.

Recent findings suggest that integration with CI/CD pipelines extends coverage to infrastructure-as-code templates before they reach production. Drift detection then monitors running clusters for any post-deployment changes that reintroduce weak bindings or unencrypted secrets. Organizations that adopt this layered validation reduce the attack surface that incidents like the Rackspace breach exploited, replacing periodic reviews with persistent, machine-enforced guardrails.

In Kubernetes environments exposed by the Rackspace Spot breach, Layer 7 routing rules implemented through ingress controllers or service meshes can inspect HTTP headers, paths, and JWT claims before traffic reaches secret stores. Hardened policies reject requests lacking specific authorization tokens or originating from unapproved pod labels, preventing lateral movement that allowed extraction of customer credentials.

Operators define per-route access lists that map only to designated namespaces holding sensitive ConfigMaps and Secrets. For instance, an Envoy filter can enforce that GET requests to /v1/secrets require both mTLS identity validation and a matching RBAC annotation, dropping all other flows at the edge before they traverse the cluster network.

In a recent development, this approach creates least-privilege boundaries by combining path-based routing with header rewriting that strips sensitive metadata from unauthorized callers. When combined with service mesh policy enforcement, clusters limit secret access to workloads explicitly declared in the mesh configuration, reducing the blast radius of any single compromised pod.

Audit logs generated at the Layer 7 layer record every denied request with source workload identity, enabling rapid detection of anomalous patterns that precede secret exfiltration attempts.

Sources indicate that following incidents where exposed credentials allowed unauthorized entry into container orchestration environments, teams must prioritize rapid hardening of cluster configurations. Begin by auditing all service accounts and removing overly permissive roles that could expose sensitive data such as API tokens or environment variables stored in secrets.

Enabling continuous scanning across workloads and infrastructure components detects misconfigurations and drift in real time. Automated tools should integrate directly into CI/CD pipelines to flag issues like unencrypted secrets or open network policies before deployment, providing ongoing visibility rather than periodic checks that leave windows of exposure.

Deploying policy-driven load balancers adds another layer by enforcing granular traffic rules and zero-trust segmentation at the application edge. These controls can automatically isolate compromised pods and restrict lateral movement even if initial access occurs through stolen secrets.

LSE CenTest combined with the LSE Layer 7 load balancer delivers integrated scanning and policy enforcement tailored for Kubernetes environments, allowing teams to validate configurations continuously while maintaining strict access boundaries at the ingress layer.

In a recent development, teams navigating the issues above don't have to solve them from scratch. LSE CenTest security/compliance platform and the LSE Layer 7 load balancer was built for exactly this kind of operational challenge, giving teams a practical path forward without reinventing the wheel in-house.

published: false description: A step-by-step guide to running a Docker container bound to localhost, routing traffic through Nginx, and automating HTTPS with Let's Encrypt on Ubuntu 24.04.

Industry observers note that running a containerized web application directly on a public port like :3000 or :8080 works during local development, but it creates serious security and reliability gaps in production. Exposing a container port directly to the internet leaves your traffic unencrypted over plain HTTP, makes managing multiple services on a single server difficult, and bypasses reverse-proxy protections like rate limiting and clean header forwarding.

In this guide, you will deploy a containerized web service on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server using a production-ready architecture. Instead of exposing the container to the public internet, you will bind it strictly to 127.0.0.1, route incoming requests through Nginx, and secure your domain with an auto-renewing Let's Encrypt SSL certificate.

By the end of this tutorial, all external traffic will follow this request flow:.

Before you begin, make sure you have:.

Note: Replace ://yourdomain.com with your actual domain name throughout every command and configuration file in this tutorial.

Start by updating your server's package index and installing the prerequisite packages needed to add Docker's official repository alongside Nginx.

Next, add Docker's official GPG key and repository so you install the maintained Docker Engine rather than an outdated distribution package:.

Add your non-root user to the docker group so you can manage containers without prefixing every command with sudo:.

Now configure UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) to allow SSH connections and standard web traffic (80 and 443 via the Nginx Full profile) while blocking all other incoming ports:.

Verify both your firewall rules and Docker installation:.

You should see output confirming that ports 22, 80, and 443 are open and Docker is installed:.

When developers run docker run -p 8080:80 ..., Docker binds port 8080 to 0.0.0.0 (every network interface on the host) and automatically modifies iptables rules—often bypassing UFW completely. That means anyone who knows your server's IP address could visit http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:8080 and bypass Nginx and HTTPS altogether.

To prevent this, explicitly bind the host port to 127.0.0.1 so only processes running on the same server (like Nginx) can reach the container.

Launch a lightweight demo web container (nginxdemos/hello) bound strictly to localhost:.

Here is what each flag accomplishes:.

Confirm the container is running and responds locally:.

Now configure Nginx to accept public requests for ://yourdomain.com and forward them internally to http://127.0.0.1:8080.

Create a dedicated server block configuration file in /etc/nginx/sites-available/:.

Paste the following configuration, replacing ://yourdomain.com with your actual domain:.

It has been revealed that save and close the file (Ctrl + O, Enter, Ctrl + X in nano). Next, enable the site by creating a symbolic link in sites-enabled, remove the default welcome site if you no longer need it, and test your Nginx syntax:.

If the configuration test succeeds, reload Nginx to apply the changes:.

Verify that your domain now serves the containerized application over HTTP:.

With HTTP routing confirmed, use Certbot to problem a free TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt and automatically configure Nginx to redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.

Install Certbot and its Nginx plugin:.

Once validated, Certbot modifies /etc/nginx/sites-available/://yourdomain.com to attach your SSL certificate and enable automatic HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection.

First, verify that HTTP requests now return a 301 Moved Permanently redirect to HTTPS:.

Next, confirm that Certbot's scheduled systemd timer will renew your certificate automatically before its 90-day expiration:.

If you see Congratulations, all simulated renewals succeeded, your TLS automation is ready for production.

Even with clean configs, two issues commonly trip up fresh deployments:.

A 502 Bad Gateway means Nginx is reachable, but it cannot connect to your upstream container on 127.0.0.1:8080.

Let's Encrypt must connect to your server over port 80 to verify domain ownership.

You now have a containerized web application running behind an Nginx reverse proxy on Ubuntu 24.04, isolated from direct public port access and encrypted with automated Let's Encrypt SSL certificates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

This feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

This auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

Sources indicate that on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with new experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

Sources indicate that the CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq shows how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

It has been revealed that CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

Groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

To make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling customers to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

We've introduced a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

Industry observers note that CUGA brings a new level of flexibility and openness to AI agent building. To engage with us:.

The structured planning, tool orchestration, and benchmark results demonstrate a strong approach to scalable agent design. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI builders love public storage buckets. They make image uploads "just work": no policies, no signed URLs, no errors. That's fine for logos and avatars. It's not fine when the same bucket holds ID photos, invoices, contracts or anything a user uploaded expecting it to stay private.

Keep public buckets for public things only. Put private uploads in a bucket with Public off, stored under the user's id (/invoice.pdf), with owner-only policies:.

Show files with short-lived signed URLs instead of permanent public links:.

Then remove broad select policies from public buckets (public files load without one; the policy mostly adds listing), and move existing sensitive files: copy to the private bucket, patch paths in your database, delete the public copies.

The full guide, with FAQs, is on LeakPatrol. If you want an outside check of your live app (leaked keys, public files, tables that answer without a login), there's a free read-only scan there too.

  • Feel free to ping me on LinkedIn if you are also intrigued by the intricacies of computer systems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I am Pavitar. A Software Engineer with knack for understanding and owning systems. You will see me larping about Distributed systems in my LeetCode t-shirt, bragging about my Leetcode achievements (not many yet), grinding on Codeforces and writing deep dives on Concurrency and Systems concepts.

Feel free to ping me on LinkedIn if you are also intrigued by the intricacies of computer systems.

We are going to try to understand the design decisions made in this blog post.

Shopify Engineering Blog: https://shopify.engineering/scaling-inventory-reservations.

Recent findings suggest that I have been seeing lots of post on LinkedIn about this migration blog. I also saw comments asking some deep question. So, I thought of starting my blogging journey with a deep dive on how Shopify did it. In my humble opinion, their article does an amazing job of hiding the complex decision made and the reasoning behind it.

Let's first list down the problem of Inventory reservation, which Shopify was trying to do better on.

It has been revealed that all E-commerce apps need to reserve inventory when you make a purchase. Normal purchase flow is Customer adding some X SKUs (items) in varying quantity to my cart. Customer clicks Pay/Checkout and these items are reserved unless I complete the purchase or the transaction times out (let's say 15 minutes after I clicked buy now).

It has been revealed that this ain't the only way though. There are other ways to achieve this, go explore some books or ask your favourite AI agent.

Before this migration, Shopify used the classic pattern of Redis as the quantity counter and SQL (mySQL here) database as ultimate source of truth.

Reserving some items means you run a LUA script. Restore if the transaction didn't finish.

Recent findings suggest that one main matter with this is quite classic. How do you make the operation atomic?

According to recent reports, see. It is not as easy as those Youtube Videos seems to imply.

It has been revealed that but why? My single server eCommerce app has no such challenges when I started to learn (way before AI, lucky me).

I mean, you can always get an ice-cream and forget that issues happen. We will care, when they happen. Let's just ship.

Sources indicate that ok, seriously. What if mySQL could be used? But everyone knows that single row for each SKU doesn't scale.

Recent findings suggest that each row need to be locked. Suppose 100 people simultaneously want Wired Headphones (I want one). The query would be something like:.

Sources indicate that this query looks innocent. But it's not. mySQL (InnoDB) has REPEATBALE_READ as default isolation level.

Industry observers note that under REPEATABLE READ InnoDB ensures that this upgrade is reproducible; it will always affect the same records because it blocks any other statements from impacting the results. While this transaction is open, no other client may INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE a record whose value overlaps this query.

The consequences of the above paragraphs are large. Transaction wait in line to revision a SKU. If you purchased 3 SKUs, you are amplify the waiting by 3 rows. More rows you touch, more contention you cause.

Sounds boring, right? We will see shortly.

Shopify Engineers did something clever. It is so obvious but you won't think of it unless you (not your AI model 😝) have deep knowledge of how Databases work under the hood (read some books, boring things). Shopify split the the SKU quantity into individual rows.

According to recent reports, but this is not without problems. Listing some obvious problems.

Before we get to how they solved some of these, let's understand their Database Schema for the product table.

They have shop_id , inventory_item_id and inventory_group_id as main fields mentioned.

Industry observers note that this is inventory management system. So, you need to have the following queries fast:.

Recent findings suggest that there is a obvious hierarchy here. First thing you will search with is shop_id and ask for a specific inventory_item_id. I don't have any clue about usage of inventory_group_id, so I will just keep it at last.

This is where Composite Primary Key fits in. It is created with shop_id , inventory_item_id and inventory_group_id in the same order + ID field (why? Keep reading).

Industry observers note that let me speed this up a bit. All the rows need to have a natural order for database to store. If you don't provide a Primay key, it creates it's own internal Primary Key as it is needed to store the data in some order.

In a recent development, this Primary Key is used to create Clustered Index. Clustered Index defines the order in which rows are ordered when stored (physically in the B-tree Pages).

A non-clustered Index is just index on a specific column with pointers to Clustered Index. Thus, row insertion, deletion or updation need to patch the clustered index as well as the non-clustered indexes. (See, this is why indexes make write slower databases).

Shopify team mentions that they tried using UUID before settling for the above Composite Primary Key.

Why wouldn't UUID work? Well, there are quite a few problems:.

So, the stage is set for a composite index. But why would the last part of composite key be id? To satisfy the Uniqueness constraints of Clustered index. And to count the quantities, you cannot have more than a specific number of rows per item. Else, think about 10k rows for a low value high moving item. it will fill up so many pages.

It has been revealed that I see. Too addicted to those summarisation by AI. Let's go through what we know:.

Industry observers note that too much info to digest, right? Let me give you a break and some reference resources to go through, before we get to the 2nd Part.

In a recent development, my favorite is Database Internals by Alex Petrov. Read the first section. Take your time.

If curious, read upto transaction management. You will understand deeply about how row locking work.

As for how InnoDB locking work, Check out this Blog (Mentioned by Shopify Blog).
