Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Sources indicate that similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Sources indicate that multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

It has been revealed that VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

Sources indicate that some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

In a recent development, the model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

Recent findings suggest that with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

In a recent development, as expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

In a recent development, you might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

Recent findings suggest that for retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

According to recent reports, under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

In a recent development, multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The presently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

It has been revealed that the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

Industry observers note that the "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

Recent findings suggest that in Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

The training companion to this post and adjacent Sentence Transformers guides:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most creators write the title first, then ask for a thumbnail that "pops". The result is often the same sentence twice: the title claims "How to edit on your phone" and the thumbnail says "Edit on phone". Viewers get one idea for the price of two.

The youtube-title-thumbnail-brief skill for Hermes starts from your idea and what the video really reveals. It proposes five pairs, each with a title, a short thumbnail text, and a one-sentence visual description. The angles differ: a test, a mistake to avoid, a before/after, a question.

Then a small checker reads your candidates and flags the usual problems:.

Fix the lines, run it again, and you get OK: no problems found. The skill then writes a short brief for your designer: what to keep, what to leave out, the exact text.

According to recent reports, it needs only Python 3, no account and no key. The limits are guidelines, not platform rules, and the checker can't tell you which pair your audience will click. Test your two best options and read your own analytics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#103472. Implementing idempotency in distributed systems: patterns and pitfalls

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (667 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Implementing idempotency in distributed systems: patterns and pitfalls

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Distributed systems fail in partial ways.
  • In a recent development, an operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times produces the same result as applying it once.
  • Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to prevent duplicate requests — networks are unreliable and clients will retry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Distributed systems fail in partial ways. A network timeout does not tell you whether the request arrived, executed, and was lost on the way back — or never arrived at all. Without idempotency, retrying that request can double-charge a customer, send the same email twice, or insert duplicate records. This article covers the practical patterns you need and the traps most teams fall into.

In a recent development, an operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times produces the same result as applying it once. DELETE /people/42 is naturally idempotent: deleting an already-deleted user returns 404 but leaves the system in the same state. POST /payments is not: a naive implementation creates a new payment on each call.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to prevent duplicate requests — networks are unreliable and clients will retry. The goal is to make duplicates safe.

The most common approach for POST endpoints is the idempotency key: the client generates a unique key (usually UUID v4), sends it as a header, and the server deduplicates on it.

Here is a minimal implementation in Go using PostgreSQL:.

Two things worth noting: store the full response — status code and body — not just a "done" flag. Replaying the exact original response is what makes the client treat the duplicate as a no-op. Also store error responses; if the card was declined, the client needs to know that, not receive a silent 200 on retry.

Recent findings suggest that for some operations you can skip a separate idempotency store entirely. If a payment's ID is derived from hash(user_id + date + amount), inserting the same payment twice hits the same primary key and fails gracefully.

This works well for batch imports and event processing. It does not work when the same operation can legitimately recur (charging the same amount on two different days).

In a recent development, idempotency collapses when you need to write to a database and publish an event. The classic failure: you commit the DB write, then crash before publishing — or you publish, then the write fails.

The outbox pattern keeps everything in one transaction:.

According to recent reports, the DB write is atomic. The publish is at-least-once, so consumer deduplication is still required — but at least you will never lose an event.

Checking idempotency after the side effect. The check must happen before any external call. If you call your payment processor first and then check the idempotency store, you have already charged the card before deduplicating.

According to recent reports, not purging old records. An idempotency store that grows forever is a liability. Stripe retains keys for 24 hours. Set a TTL that covers your retry window and schedule a cleanup:.

Recent findings suggest that assuming your dependencies are idempotent. Each layer of a distributed call chain needs its own idempotency key, passed through. An idempotent API can still trigger non-idempotent downstream calls.

Using timestamps or client IPs as keys. Timestamps collide under load; IPs are shared. Keys must be client-generated UUIDs with enough entropy — typically UUID v4.

Treating Kafka producer idempotency as enough. enable.idempotence=true prevents duplicate messages within one producer session but does not survive restarts. Consumer-side deduplication is still required.

Industry observers note that idempotency is not an edge case — it is a design requirement for every distributed write that might be retried, which is all of them. The pattern is simple: client-generated key, server-side result storage, exact response replay. The complexity comes from TTLs, error handling, ordering of checks, and propagating keys through call chains. Getting this right before production is cheaper than debugging duplicate payments after.

If you are running an audit of your API's resilience posture, the free architecture and security checklists we publish cover idempotency alongside authentication, rate limiting, and input validation — in a format you can hand to a team.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

#103471. Tech Report: Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1738 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

It has been revealed that granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Industry observers note that figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

In a recent development, the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

In a recent development, figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

According to recent reports, our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

Industry observers note that we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

It has been revealed that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

It has been revealed that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

Industry observers note that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that we use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

In a recent development, figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

It has been revealed that in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

It has been revealed that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

In a recent development, to mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

Recent findings suggest that during our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

It has been revealed that figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

Sources indicate that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

#103469. The Agent Found the Zero-Day by Itself

The Agent Found the Zero-Day by Itself

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somewhere between the prompt and the payload, the human stopped choosing the next step — and that single change is about to rewrite how we talk about AI-driven hacking.
  • For most of a year, the honest description of AI-driven hacking was that it had become faster, not different.
  • That loop broke this month, in public, with receipts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somewhere between the prompt and the payload, the human stopped choosing the next step — and that single change is about to rewrite how we talk about AI-driven hacking.

For most of a year, the honest description of AI-driven hacking was that it had become faster, not different. A researcher picked a target, prompted a model, read the output, and chose the next step. The model was quicker. The loop was still human, and a human choosing the next step is the thing that keeps most of these stories from being stories.

That loop broke this month, in public, with receipts.

On November 20, Amazon's own threat intelligence team published the operational history of an intrusion that nobody was steering. Somewhere in the middle of it is an AI agent that found a vulnerability that did not previously exist, exploited it, and escalated to root — in about eleven minutes, from a cold start, with no human choosing anything.

It has been revealed that the story starts with a mistake. On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence noticed a server running a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, with no authentication on it. Because the operator left it reachable, the entire operational history was visible to anyone who knew where to look: project configurations, the actor's prompts, and the raw model output.

Recent findings suggest that that is the kind of operational-security failure that normally gets an operator a visit from their own side. Here it handed a cloud provider the most detailed record yet of what an agent-driven intrusion actually looks like when nobody is holding the wheel.

The prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, and timestamps in the executed scripts were set to China Standard Time. The actor gave the agents a list of target IPs and one instruction in plain language: obtain shell access. Everything after that — reconnaissance, the attempt chains, the retries, the pivot to the next technique — was the agents' own work. Amazon assesses with moderate confidence this is a Chinese-nexus actor, citing the language, the timezone, and a target list of universities likely to be of strategic interest.

The operation that failed is the one worth reading.

The most revealing operation in the report is the one where the agents got nowhere.

Against a Redis instance at one university, they worked for roughly sixteen hours and took 148 sequential actions. They abused Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaped its scripting sandbox, wrote to its configuration files, and corrupted its memory. When those attempts failed, they tried Log4Shell injection against a co-located service, mapped the internal Docker network through a server-side request forgery flaw in a neighbouring Qdrant instance, and ran credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH and others.

A second operation ran more than six hours against a university GPU server. The agents harvested roughly eighty real usernames from faculty directories, lab websites, archived pages and academic papers, then tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against exposed services — a machine-scale version of exactly what a human red team does by hand, only without the coffee break.

According to recent reports, that failure is the point. The run that succeeded — the eleven-minute chain that ended in root — is the headline, but the boring sixteen-hour slog is what tells you something important: agents do not just scale up. They chain techniques, they fall back, they re-plan. The same reasoning loop that produced a zero-day also produced sixteen hours of nothing. Capability and patience arrive together.

It has been revealed that for defenders, the practical questions are uncomfortable. If an agent can find and exploit a vulnerability that did not previously exist, does your vulnerability management process assume a human is reading every alert? If a single instruction — obtain shell access — is enough to start a chain of 148 actions against your infrastructure, what does your detection actually look for: the exploits, or the attempts?

According to recent reports, we have spent years asking whether AI would change offensive security. The answer, it turns out, was never really about the AI. It was about who was in the loop.

This was first published on Sol AI — https://thesolai.github.io.

Florian Lamm of Lamm & Kirch pairs OT Scholar type with Attila Hartwigâs photos in the Best Book Design 2026 Leipzig prize catalog.

Industry observers note that there isnât a horizontal cover title anywhere on the front board. Designed by Florian Lamm of Leipzig studio Lamm & Kirch for Stiftung Buchkunst, the catalog for Best Book Design from All over the World 2026 shifts its name onto a narrow white fore-edge step along the right margin. Single upright capitals stack cleanly from top to bottom, ending in the year 2026 at the foot. On page 1, photographer Attila Hartwig curls a dark softcover volume into a tight loop so its fanned leaves catch an upward flare of studio light. Nothing sits flat on a white seamless sweep. Turn to pages 4 and 5 and a pinched black binding angled like a boat prow faces the hazy shadow silhouette of Anthology for Listening Vol. II, while page 14 captures an open wire-stitched gutter throwing a candle-like reflection straight up the grey sheet.

Opposite page 14, Omnitypeâs OT Scholar takes command of the directory. Three narrow columns sort national prize winners submitted from more than thirty countries, building a competition archive that traces its Leipzig roots back to 1963 without needing a single ruled divider line. Winners get solid black numbered dots. Fourteen awardees, led by Dutch Goldene Letter recipient Ouroboros Wings, French Gold Medal winner Picalso, and Silver Medal titles Odes and Sophie Thun: Zwischen Licht und Wand, carry white numerals inside black discs â while shortlisted books below wear hollow hairline rings.

It has been revealed that that three-column grid holds steady across every country section, from Belgium and Canada to China, Austria, and Hungary. Inside each narrow column, left-aligned roman labels for Title, Author/Editor, Publisher, Design, Illustration/Photography, Printer, and ISBN hang clean beside italic book titles and thirteen-digit numbers. Dense Hungarian, Czech, and German diacritics stay sharp even at compact catalog sizes. Whenever a listed book wins a medal, its numbered black dot and jury commentary drop right inline above paired monochrome object photos anchored at the lower margin. Faint show-through across the thin uncoated pages gives this book design catalog the quiet utility of a working Leipzig Book Fair reference.

#103463. Twenty-seven answers per prompt: the curation work behind a daily answer game

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (735 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Twenty-seven answers per prompt: the curation work behind a daily answer game

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That makes the content cheap to build and cheap to check: type a word, compare it to a string, done.
  • One prompt, two minutes, about 27 hidden answers to name.
  • That format is easy to describe and annoying to build, because every part of it depends on a list that has to be right before the round opens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most daily games hide one answer. That makes the content cheap to build and cheap to check: type a word, compare it to a string, done. We went the other direction, and the work moved from the game loop into the answer bank.

One prompt, two minutes, about 27 hidden answers to name. You get points for each answer you find, and the points depend on how rare the answer is, not on how many you found. Seven hints are free. The next prompt appears at 00:00 UTC.

That format is easy to describe and annoying to build, because every part of it depends on a list that has to be right before the round opens.

"Name things you would find in a kitchen drawer" sounds like a five-minute job. It is not. You have to decide, for a single prompt, what counts as an answer, what counts as a duplicate, and what counts as too obscure to accept.

Take batteries. Is a "dead battery" a separate answer from "battery"? No. Is "AA battery" separate? It is the same object, so also no. Is "battery charger" separate? Yes, it is a different object. Multiply that conversation by 27 entries and 120 prompts in the bank and you have the actual content pipeline.

It has been revealed that every prompt sits in the bank with its answer list, its rarity weights and its hint ladder before it can go live. An answer bank that is 90 percent right is worse than useless: the player who types the missing legitimate answer gets a miss, and a miss feels like the game is broken rather than like the player is wrong.

The matching layer has to forgive the things people cannot control and refuse the things they can.

Industry observers note that forgiven: capitalisation, extra spaces, punctuation, accents, leading articles ("the", "a", "an"), and simple plurals in both directions. "Batteries" and "battery" are the same answer.

In a recent development, not forgiven: a different word. "Charger" is not "battery charger". If the game accepted loose semantic matches, scores would depend on how generous the matcher happened to be that day, and the whole rarity system would inherit that noise.

Duplicates never score twice, which sounds obvious until you watch someone type the same answer three ways in a two-minute round.

Every answer carries a weight from 1 to 5:.

According to recent reports, your score is the sum of the weights. Your tier is the weight of the rarest answer you found, not the total. Finding one Legendary, one Rare and four Commons is 12 points and a Legendary tier.

According to recent reports, that split matters in a game like this. If the tier were the total, the winning strategy would be to type as many obvious answers as possible as fast as possible, which is exactly the behaviour the game is not trying to reward. Making the tier follow the single rarest find means the two-minute clock is spent deciding whether to keep listing groceries or to reach for something odd.

In a recent development, each round has seven hints: first letters, word lengths, category clues, in that order. They cost nothing.

Free hints are a deliberate choice. Charging for them would turn a two-minute game into a resource-management game, and it would punish the player who is stuck rather than the player who is careless. Hints narrow the search space without handing over the answer, which is the only job a hint has.

When the round ends, the full board is visible: every answer, its weight and its tier. That reveal is where most of the learning happens — you see the Legendary you missed and realise it was obvious in hindsight.

Past boards stay available for 90 days, so a missed day is not a lost streak. There is no signup, no download, and no energy system, which means the only thing keeping you in the loop is whether the prompt is good.

If we rebuilt the answer bank from scratch, we would write the hint ladder first. Writing hints before the answer list forces you to describe the categories out loud, and half of the awkward entries reveal themselves at that stage, before the prompt ever reaches a player.

The daily board is at ZomZam if you want to see the finished version of this pipeline in two minutes.

📖 Baca

3 Dark Personality Traits Linked To Infidelity

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (428 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).
